title: Why a little Pali
hook: a chorus you sing by sound, until you learn what it says
tomorrow: why do chants stretch some sounds and clip others?

segments.voice: Year four closed on one street with four temple doors. Your line was many doors, one house. Year five walks through one of those doors and hands you its language.
screen: `MANY DOORS, ONE HOUSE.` → `YEAR FIVE: A LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: There's a song on your playlist in a language you don't speak. You know every sound of the chorus. You sing it in the car. Then one day you look up the lyrics, and the next time it plays, the chorus lands differently: you're singing words now, not just sounds. Theravada temples have a chorus like that. Evening chanting often opens with a line in Pali: namo tassa bhagavato. Some chant it by sound alone, and chant it well. So, one question for today: if the English is right there, why learn a little of the old language at all?
screen: `A CHORUS YOU SING BY SOUND.` → `NAMO TASSA BHAGAVATO.` → `WHY LEARN THE OLD LANGUAGE?`

segments.voice: Start with the Buddha's own answer, which is a surprise. In the monks' rule, the Vinaya, two brothers come to him, monks from a brahmin family with fine voices. Monks from every background are saying his words in their own dialects, they complain, and spoiling them. Their fix: put the teaching into the grand verse of the Vedas. The Buddha says no. He allows each monk to learn the word of the Buddha in his own dialect. The meaning comes first. So why Pali? Because the meaning came to rest somewhere. The Theravada keeps its canon in Pali, and its temples chant in it, so two people who share no other language can share one homage. And a few words open the chant from inside. You already know one. Dhamma: the teaching, the way things are, the first half of the Dhammapada's name. Pali says dhamma where Sanskrit says dharma. Jewish neighbors know this pull between old words and plain ones. The Shema opens, in the JPS 1917 English, "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The Mishnah says the Shema may be said in any language. Shared ground: both let the meaning come in your own tongue, and both keep an old one that lets strangers say the same line together. One honest difference: the Shema speaks to a people about God. The Pali homage honors a teacher who woke up, and no creator is being addressed.
screen: `LEARN IT IN YOUR OWN DIALECT.` · `PALI: WHERE THE MEANING CAME TO REST.` · `DHAMMA, DHARMA: ONE WORD.` · `HEAR, O ISRAEL, IN ANY LANGUAGE.` · then, large: `THE WORDS BEHIND THE CHANTS.`

segments.voice: Say it out loud, slowly: Pali. Then: dhamma. Say the pair three or four times, letting each word land, the way you'd practice a new friend's name, then sit and let the last sound fade into the quiet.
Pali. The language of the Theravada canon and its chants. A little of it lets you hear the words behind the sounds. Word one of a little Pali.
Keep this one: the words behind the chants, sounds that start to mean something. Year five, begun.

howItsDone: In Theravada temples, monks and lay people chant the homage, the refuges and the precepts in Pali, often with the meaning printed beside it or said after it in the local language.

fork.setup: you're a guest at a friend's family temple and the evening chant begins. the sheet has Pali on top and English underneath. you've never chanted. what do you do?
options: chant the Pali sounds with everyone, glancing down at the English.
stay silent; chanting words you can't define yet would be fake.
read the English aloud on your own while the room chants Pali.
fork.reveal: the Buddha let the meaning come in your own tongue, so the English underneath counts. the Pali is what lets a whole room say one line together. sound and meaning, side by side.

what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's two brothers and the Buddha's answer, learn it in your own dialect; so Pali is a shared tongue for the teaching, not the only door to it.

chat.says: drawing posters for the Lao temple's kids' class. they chant in Pali. should i just learn the English?
options: Learn both. The Buddha let monks learn in their own tongue; a little Pali lets you chant with the kids.
Just the English. Chanting sounds you don't understand is empty, so the Pali doesn't matter.
Just the Pali. The chant only works in the Buddha's language, and English versions don't count.
chat.meaning: The Buddha let each monk learn his words in his own dialect, so meaning comes first; Pali is the shared tongue the chants live in.

Pali.meaning: the language of the Theravada canon and its chants

dhamma.meaning: the Buddha's teaching, the way things are; dharma in Sanskrit

Theravada.meaning: the school of the elders, which keeps its canon in Pali

Vinaya.meaning: the monks' and nuns' rule, part of the canon

Shema.meaning: the Jewish declaration that begins Hear, O Israel

Mishnah.meaning: an early collection of Jewish teaching and law

notes: Vinaya Cullavagga V.33.1 (Rhys Davids and Oldenberg, Vinaya Texts III, SBE XX): two brothers of a brahmin family with fine voices (named Yamelu and Tekula in the text; names left out of the voice) ask to put the word of the Buddha into Vedic verse (chandaso); the Buddha refuses and allows it to be learned 'in one's own dialect' (sakaya niruttiya). Paraphrased. The commentary's reading of sakaya nirutti (the Buddha's own dialect vs the learner's) is debated; the script follows the reading in the Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translation. Keeper: confirm.
'Evening chanting often opens with namo tassa bhagavato' is hedged; confirm fair for Theravada temples. Its meaning is taught on days 1430–1433, so it is only sounded here.

Neighbor (Judaism): Deuteronomy 6:4 quoted from JPS 1917 ('Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.'); confirm exact wording and punctuation. Mishnah Sotah 7:1 paraphrased: the Shema may be recited in any language. The difference line (the Shema speaks to a people about God; the Pali homage honors a teacher who woke up, with no creator addressed) should be checked by both a Jewish and a Theravada reader for fairness; no ranking intended.
No claim is made about whether Pali is the Buddha's own speech; that question is left out on purpose (claims rule).
Myth item: 'other schools read their texts in other languages' points back to year four (Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan collections) without naming counts.
